title: Commission Guidelines on the Scope of the Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models (C(2025) 7719 final)

covered_actors: Providers of general-purpose AI models (within the Union and in third countries placing models on the Union market)
Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
Downstream modifiers of general-purpose AI models exceeding modification compute thresholds
Downstream providers integrating general-purpose AI models into AI systems
Authorised representatives established in the Union for third-country providers
Providers of general-purpose AI models released under free and open-source licences

evidence.quote: For this reason, the AI Act lays down proportionate transparency measures, including an obligation to draw up and keep up to date documentation to be made available to downstream providers and, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities (Article 53(1), points (a) and (b), AI Act).

Article 53(1), point (a), AI Act: the obligation to ‘draw up and keep up-todate the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation, which shall contain, at a
minimum, the information set out in Annex XI for the purpose of providing it, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities’;

the AI Act also requires providers of general-purpose AI models to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1), point (c), AI Act), and to make publicly available a summary of the content used for the training (Article 53(1), point (d), AI Act).

providers of general-purpose AI models that meet the conditions referred to in Section 4.2 are not exempted from the obligation laid down in Article 53(1), point (c), AI Act to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law.

Under the AI Act, general-purpose AI models trained with a cumulative amount of computational resources greater than 1025 floating-point operations (‘FLOP’, see Article 3(67) AI Act) are presumed to be general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 51(2) AI Act).

When a general-purpose AI model has met or it becomes known that it will meet a requirement leading to the presumption that the model has high-impact capabilities,7 the provider must notify the Commission in line with Article 52(1) AI Act (see also recital 112 AI Act).

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk are subject, in addition to the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, to obligations aimed at assessing and mitigating those risks.
The systemic risk assessment and mitigation required under Article 55(1) AI Act must be carried out continuously for each model throughout its entire lifecycle.

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk are subject, in addition to the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, to obligations aimed at assessing and mitigating those risks. These include conducting model evaluations, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection.

Whether a given general-purpose AI model has high-impact capabilities should be ‘evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks’, under Article 51(1), point (a), AI Act.
Such proactive reporting is without prejudice to the obligation to keep track of, document, and report relevant information about ‘serious incidents’ under Article 55(1), point (c), AI Act.

The AI Office considers that this obligation covers serious cybersecurity breaches related to the model or its physical infrastructure, including the (self-)exfiltration of model parameters and cyberattacks, due to their possible implications for the obligations provided for in Article 55(1), points (b) and (d), AI
Act.
They must also ‘ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, if appropriate, along the entire model lifecycle’ (recital 115 AI Act).

Nevertheless, if the model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, the fact that the model is released under a free and open-source licence is not sufficient for these obligations not to apply to its provider.

For the exceptions referred to in Section 4.1 to apply, the model’s ‘parameters, including the weights, the information on the model architecture, and the information on model usage’ must be ‘made publicly available’ (Articles 53(2) and 54(6) AI Act).

To facilitate compliance, providers established or located within a third country must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before placing a general-purpose AI model on the Union market (Article 54 AI Act).

The AI Office is tasked with supervising, investigating, enforcing, and monitoring the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models laid down in Chapter V of the AI Act (Articles 88 and 89 AI Act)

These are the powers to: (i) request information (Article 91 AI Act); (ii) conduct evaluations of general-purpose AI models (Article 92 AI Act); (iii) request measures from providers, including implementing mitigation measures and recalling the model from the market (Article 93 AI Act);
The notification must happen ‘without delay and in any event within two weeks after that requirement is met or it becomes known that it will be met’ (Article 52(1) AI Act).

Providers of general-purpose AI models that do not adhere to a code of practice that is assessed as adequate are expected to demonstrate how they comply with their obligations under Chapter V of the AI Act via other adequate means, and will have to report the measures they have implemented to the AI Office.

Providers of general-purpose AI models can demonstrate compliance with the obligations in Articles 53(1) and 55(1) AI Act by adhering to a code of practice that is assessed as adequate by the AI Office and the Board (Article 56(6) AI Act).

The Commission may take into account commitments implemented in line with a code of practice that is assessed as adequate as a mitigating factor when fixing the amount of fines, depending on the specific circumstances (Article 101(1) AI Act).

compliance_deadlines: 2025-08-02: Entry into application of Chapter V AI Act obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Article 113(b) AI Act) and Commission Article 52 designation/contest decisions.

Within two weeks after meeting or foreseeing the systemic-risk threshold (or within two weeks after 2025-08-02 for models trained or planned for placement after that date): Mandatory notification to the Commission under Article 52(1) AI Act.
2026-08-02: Entry into application of Commission enforcement powers and fines under Article 101 AI Act.
2027-08-02: Compliance deadline for general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2025-08-02 (Article 111(3) AI Act).
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Starting on 2 August 2026, the European Commission may impose fines of up to 3% of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher (Article 101 AI Act), including for failure to notify systemic-risk classification. The Commission may also request information (Article 91), conduct model evaluations (Article 92), and order mitigation measures or recall models from the market (Article 93). Adherence to a code of practice assessed as adequate may serve as a mitigating factor when fixing fines.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Non-binding interpretive guidelines adopted under Article 96(1) AI Act setting out the European Commission's enforcement interpretation for Chapter V GPAI obligations (subject to authoritative interpretation by the CJEU). Establishes indicative training-compute criteria (>10^23 FLOP with language, text-to-image, or text-to-video generation for GPAI models; >10^25 FLOP cumulative compute for systemic-risk presumption; >1/3 of original training compute for downstream modifiers), defines open-source exemption boundaries (requiring no monetisation and excluding systemic-risk models while maintaining copyright policy and training-data summary obligations), clarifies the compliance role of adequate codes of practice and harmonised standards, and outlines a collaborative, staged enforcement approach by the AI Office without requiring retraining or unlearning of pre-2 August 2025 models where impossible or disproportionate.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The guidelines frame GPAI governance primarily through innovation enablement, edging out fundamental rights and consumer/public safety because the Commission's recurring rationale for its interpretive criteria, thresholds, open-source exemptions, and enforcement posture is to promote AI innovation and uptake, limit compliance burdens on value-chain actors, avoid disincentivising model modification, and ensure timely market placement via proportionate, collaborative supervision. Fundamental rights (including democracy, rule of law, procedural rights, and personal data protection) and consumer/public safety (protecting health and public safety from systemic and operational risks) serve as major secondary justifications anchored in the underlying AI Act objectives, while economic competitiveness appears as a narrower secondary rationale tied to growth opportunities for the Union economy from open-source models.

evidence_spans.quote: Its aim is to promote innovation in and uptake of artificial intelligence (‘AI’) in the Union, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights, including democracy and the rule of law.

The AI Office will take a collaborative, staged, and proportionate approach. The AI Office encourages close informal cooperation with providers during the training of their general-purpose AI models to facilitate compliance and ensure timely market placement, in particular for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

While fully recognising that the protection of personal data is a fundamental right and that therefore personal data cannot be considered a commodity or monetised, access, use, modification, or redistribution of the model requiring the collection or otherwise processing of personal data should be treated in same manner as monetisation strategies

The AI Act defines a ‘systemic risk’ as ‘a risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain’

While the licence must generally permit use for any purpose, licensors may include specific, safety-oriented terms that reasonably restrict usage in applications or domains where such use would pose a significant risk to public safety, security, or fundamental rights.

The first is that models released under a free and open-source licence ‘can contribute to research and innovation in the market and can provide significant growth opportunities for the Union economy’ (recital 102 AI Act).
